unit.title: Introduction to Electrical Energy and DC Circuits

title: Network theorems — superposition and Thevenin’s theorem
summary: Network theorems; superposition theorem and source suppression; a corrected two-source superposition example; Thevenin’s theorem, open-circuit voltage and Thevenin resistance; and class-worked circuit calculations.
transcription_policy: Class-note order is preserved and wording is lightly cleaned for study. Crossed-out calculations are not treated as final answers. The Superposition redraws have been normalized so the original circuit and the two source-isolation sketches are internally consistent with the theorem: the original circuit is shown with both 15 V and 20 V sources, the “15 V acting alone” sketch suppresses the 20 V source by a short circuit, and the “20 V acting alone” sketch suppresses the 15 V source by a short circuit. All ten class-note redraws are integrated: the three first Superposition figures, the four Thevenin figures, and the three later 18 V / 22 V worked-network figures. For the later worked network, Priyanka’s black-ink working and the teacher’s red review marks are distinguished explicitly; the teacher-approved 18 V-alone result is retained, the red-crossed 22 V-alone result is corrected and identified as a verified PankusDesk correction, and the complete two-source result is checked independently.

blocks.text: Network theorems are useful for finding the voltage or current of one specific branch. This simplifies the use of mesh or nodal analysis, which can otherwise produce simultaneous equations involving other voltages and currents in addition to the required one.
In a linear network containing two or more sources, the response in any element is equal to the algebraic sum of the responses caused by the individual sources acting alone.
Voltage source → replace with a short circuit when it is made non-operative.
Current source → replace with an open circuit when it is made non-operative.
Ideal current source: internal resistance \(\to\infty\). Ideal voltage source: internal resistance \(=0\).

items.title: What the theorem means here
paragraphs: Superposition theorem is used when a linear circuit has more than one independent source. Instead of solving the full circuit at once, we find the required response due to one source at a time and then add the individual responses algebraically.

A voltage source that is made non-operative is replaced by a short circuit because an ideal voltage source has zero internal resistance. A current source that is made non-operative is replaced by an open circuit because an ideal current source has infinite internal resistance.
bullets: Original circuit: keep both sources active.
15 V acting alone: keep the 15 V source, suppress the 20 V source by a short circuit.
20 V acting alone: keep the 20 V source, suppress the 15 V source by a short circuit.
Final response: add the separate contributions with the correct sign.

paragraphs: The first redraw is the original two-source network. The left branch contains the 15 V source, the right branch contains the 20 V source, the top branch has 1 kΩ and 2.2 kΩ resistors, and the centre branch has a 3.3 kΩ resistor.

In the notebook, the right-hand source in the original sketch is not clearly labeled, but the next class-note sketch explicitly says “When 20 V is acting alone”. That is why the corrected redraw labels the original right-hand source as 20 V.
The second redraw shows the 15 V source acting alone, so the 20 V source is replaced by a short. The third redraw shows the 20 V source acting alone, so the 15 V source is replaced by a short.

items.title: How the written equations match the sketches
paragraphs: When 15 V acts alone, the current through the 1 kΩ branch is written as \((15-V)/1\). The node voltage \(V\) drives current through the 3.3 kΩ and 2.2 kΩ branches, giving the class-note relation \(15-V=V/3.3+V/2.2\). The division by 1 is omitted in the notebook because the resistance is 1 kΩ.

When 20 V acts alone, the 15 V source is shorted, so the 1 kΩ and 3.3 kΩ branches are both connected from the node to the return line. That gives the class-note relation \((20-V)/2.2=V+V/3.3\), where \(V\) again stands for \(V/1\).
bullets: The equations are consistent with the corrected redraws.
The redrawn sketches are intended to make the class-note working readable, not to invent a different example.

blocks.text: Any two-terminal linear bilateral network can be replaced by an equivalent circuit consisting of an equivalent source \(V_{th}\) (or \(V_{oc}\)) in series with resistance \(R_{th}\).
\(V_{th}\) or \(V_{oc}\): open-circuit voltage measured between the load terminals.
\(R_{th}\): Thevenin resistance seen from the load terminals with the independent sources replaced by their internal resistances.

blocks.text: Worked two-source network — second superposition example

Although this worked network appears after the Thevenin notes, the source-by-source calculation shown in the notebook uses the superposition procedure introduced earlier. It has the same resistor pattern as the earlier \(15\,\text{V}\) / \(20\,\text{V}\) example — \(1\,\text{k}\Omega\), \(2.2\,\text{k}\Omega\) and \(3.3\,\text{k}\Omega\) — but the source values are now \(18\,\text{V}\) and \(22\,\text{V}\).

blocks.label: Source model
blocks.title: Why are the 18 V and 22 V sources treated as ideal here?
paragraphs: The source symbol by itself does not prove that a voltage source is ideal, and the fact that no internal resistance is drawn is not enough by itself to prove it either.

The reason we use the ideal-source model here comes from the class-note method immediately preceding these examples: the notes state that an ideal voltage source has zero internal resistance and that a voltage source made non-operative for superposition is replaced by a short circuit. This worked example follows that same model for both the \(18\,\text{V}\) and \(22\,\text{V}\) independent sources.

Suppressing an independent voltage source means setting its source voltage to zero. For an ideal voltage source, \(R_{\text{internal}}=0\), so a zero-volt ideal source is electrically just a wire. That is why the suppressed source becomes a short circuit.

If the question had specified a practical source with a non-zero internal resistance, only the ideal source voltage would be set to zero; the stated internal resistance would remain in the circuit. We would not replace that whole branch by a plain wire.
bullets: Do not infer “ideal” merely from the battery/source symbol.
Here “ideal” is the source model used by the class-note superposition procedure.
Ideal voltage source suppressed → set \(V_s=0\) → short circuit.
Practical source suppressed → source voltage set to zero, but any stated internal resistance remains.

blocks.label: Source-note clarification
blocks.title: Why this looks familiar
paragraphs: This is essentially the same network pattern used in the earlier superposition example on these class notes. The resistor values are unchanged: \(1\,\text{k}\Omega\), \(2.2\,\text{k}\Omega\) and \(3.3\,\text{k}\Omega\). Only the source values change from \(15\,\text{V},20\,\text{V}\) to \(18\,\text{V},22\,\text{V}\).
That means the logical method is the same: analyse the response due to one independent source while suppressing the other, then analyse the second source, and finally add the signed contributions.
The full two-source node equation is not the first superposition step. It is kept as an independent check after the two individual contributions have been found.
bullets: Same resistor topology as the earlier example.
Different source values only.
Case 1: \(18\,\text{V}\) active, \(22\,\text{V}\) suppressed.
Case 2: \(22\,\text{V}\) active, \(18\,\text{V}\) suppressed.
Final response = algebraic sum of the two source contributions.

blocks.label: Step logic
blocks.title: Case 1 — why the 22 V source becomes a wire and where the KCL equation comes from
paragraphs: The \(18\,\text{V}\) source remains active. The \(22\,\text{V}\) source is the one being suppressed, so in this ideal-source model it becomes a short circuit. The \(2.2\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistor does not disappear; its right-hand end is now connected directly to the common return through that short.

Look only at node \(V\). Current arrives at the node from the \(18\,\text{V}\) source through the \(1\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistor. From node \(V\), current can leave through two paths: downward through \(3.3\,\text{k}\Omega\), and to the right through \(2.2\,\text{k}\Omega\) to the shorted return.
Using \(I=(V_1-V_2)/R\), the current entering from the left is \((18-V)/1\). The two currents leaving are \(V/3.3\) and \(V/2.2\). KCL therefore gives current entering = current leaving.
bullets: \((18-V)/1\): current entering node \(V\) from the active 18 V source.
\(V/3.3\): current leaving node \(V\) through the centre branch.
\(V/2.2\): current leaving node \(V\) through the branch created when the 22 V source is shorted.
Because voltage is in volts and resistance is in \(\text{k}\Omega\), the numerical current comes out in mA.

blocks.text: At node \(V\), with resistance in \(\text{k}\Omega\) and current therefore in mA:
This is the result beside which the teacher has placed a red tick.
Now keep the \(22\,\text{V}\) source active. In the same ideal-source model, set the \(18\,\text{V}\) source to zero volts, so that source is replaced by a short circuit.

blocks.label: Step logic
blocks.title: Case 2 — why the 18 V source becomes a wire and how the current directions change
paragraphs: This time the \(22\,\text{V}\) source remains active and the \(18\,\text{V}\) source is suppressed. The suppressed ideal source becomes a short, so the left side of the \(1\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistor is connected to the common return.

At node \(V\), current now arrives from the active \(22\,\text{V}\) source through the \(2.2\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistor. Current leaves node \(V\) through the \(1\,\text{k}\Omega\) branch on the left and through the \(3.3\,\text{k}\Omega\) branch downward.

So the entering current is \((22-V)/2.2\), while the leaving currents are \(V/1\) and \(V/3.3\). This is why the second KCL equation has a different arrangement from the first even though the resistor network is the same.
bullets: \((22-V)/2.2\): current entering node \(V\) from the active 22 V source.
\(V/1\): current leaving node \(V\) through the left branch to the shorted return.
\(V/3.3\): current leaving node \(V\) through the centre branch.
A quick KCL substitution is a good way to catch the arithmetic error in the black-ink result.

blocks.label: Verified correction
blocks.title: The lower black-ink result is not consistent with this circuit
paragraphs: Priyanka’s lower working gives approximately \(V=9.55\,\text{V}\) and \(I=2.89\,\text{mA}\). Those values do not satisfy the \(22\,\text{V}\)-alone circuit shown above.
The corrected result is \(V\approx5.69\,\text{V}\) and \(I_{22}\approx1.72\,\text{mA}\). This is the calculation over which the teacher has placed the large red correction mark.

blocks.text: Both individual contributions drive current downward through the \(3.3\,\text{k}\Omega\) branch, so the contributions add algebraically.

blocks.label: Step logic
blocks.title: Why the two superposition contributions are added, not subtracted
paragraphs: Superposition is an algebraic sum, so direction matters. We use the same downward reference direction through the \(3.3\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistor in both source-isolation cases.

The \(18\,\text{V}\)-alone calculation gives a downward contribution \(I_{18}\), and the \(22\,\text{V}\)-alone calculation also gives a downward contribution \(I_{22}\). Because both have the same sign relative to the chosen downward reference, they add.
If one source had produced current upward through the \(3.3\,\text{k}\Omega\) resistor, that contribution would have the opposite sign and the algebraic sum would effectively subtract it.
bullets: \(I_{18}\approx3.10\,\text{mA}\) downward.
\(I_{22}\approx1.72\,\text{mA}\) downward.
Therefore \(I_{\text{total}}=I_{18}+I_{22}\).

blocks.text: Independent check with both sources active

blocks.label: Check
blocks.title: Why solve the original circuit again after using superposition?
paragraphs: This is an independent verification step. Superposition should give exactly the same final response as solving the complete linear circuit with both independent sources active at the same time.

With both sources active, current reaches node \(V\) from the \(18\,\text{V}\) side through \(1\,\text{k}\Omega\) and from the \(22\,\text{V}\) side through \(2.2\,\text{k}\Omega\). The current leaving node \(V\) is \(V/3.3\) through the centre branch.

If this direct solution disagreed materially with the source-by-source total, we would know that a sign, source-suppression step, or arithmetic operation was wrong. Here they agree; the tiny \(4.82\) versus \(4.83\,\text{mA}\) difference comes only from rounding the individual contributions before adding them.

blocks.text: The \(4.82\,\text{mA}\) obtained by adding the two rounded source contributions and the \(4.83\,\text{mA}\) obtained by solving the complete circuit differ only because the individual contributions were rounded before addition.
